explain.say: See the first box, brain sorts? Your brain loves shortcuts. It sorts things into groups, like dogs or chairs, so you do not have to think hard every time. That is useful for chairs, but people are not chairs. Can you think of a group your brain sorts quickly?

explain.say: See label sticks? Now the idea becomes "they are all like that". A stereotype is a fixed idea that everyone in a group is the same. It skips over the fact that every person is different. Is anyone in your family exactly like everyone else?

explain.say: Last, look at hard to see. Once you hold a stereotype, you notice people who fit it and forget those who do not, so it feels even more true. Well done! The good news: noticing the shortcut is the first step to stopping it. Next time you make a quick picture, ask, is that really true of everyone?

faq.a: A stereotype is a fixed, oversimplified idea that everyone in a group is the same, like "all girls like pink" or "all old people are bad with phones". It ignores that every person is different.

faq.q: Why does the brain make stereotypes?
faq.a: Your brain sorts the world into groups to save time and effort. That shortcut helps with objects, but with people it can turn into wrong guesses about whole groups.
They often come from repeated pictures in films, adverts, jokes and things we hear from others, more than from real people we know. Hearing something many times makes it feel true.

faq.q: Why are stereotypes hard to get rid of?
faq.a: Once we hold one, we notice examples that fit it and forget examples that do not. This keeps the stereotype feeling true, even when it is wrong.
asks: Tell me about hard to see

faq.a: Yes, like "all people from one country are good at maths". But even a positive stereotype puts pressure on people and ignores who they really are, so it is still unfair.
asks: Is a nice stereotype still bad?

facts: The word stereotype first meant a metal printing plate that printed the same image over and over; journalist Walter Lippmann used it for fixed ideas about people in 1922.
In "draw a scientist" studies from the 1960s and 70s, fewer than 1 in 100 children drew a woman; by the 2010s it was about 3 in 10 (Miller and others, 2018).

quiz.say: Which of these is a stereotype?
quiz.why: It claims that everyone in a group is the same, which is what a stereotype does.

wrong.0: This is about one real person, not a whole group.
wrong.2: Saying "some" allows for differences, so it is not a fixed idea about everyone.
